origin_region: Altai Krai · Siberia (where modern cultivation was developed); the shrub grows from Europe to Mongolia and China, and the café drink is popular across Ukraine, Russia and Central Asia
cultivar: Hippophae rhamnoides, the bright orange berries; the leaves are also dried for a separate, milder infusion
processing: The berries are picked or shaken from the thorny branches, often after frost, then frozen, crushed or blended with sugar or honey into a purée; the café version is crushed berries topped with hot water, honey, and often ginger, orange or cinnamon. Dried berries and dried leaf are sold for conventional steeping.
harvest_season: Late August to October; many pickers wait for the first frost, when the berries loosen and sweeten slightly. Frozen berries and purée are sold all year.
appearance_dry: Plump, bright orange, oily berries (fresh or frozen); dried berries are shrivelled and dark orange; the leaf is narrow and silver-green.
appearance_liquor: Cloudy bright orange with tiny droplets of oil on the surface.
appearance_wet: Crushed pulp and skins at the bottom of the glass.
taste_profile: Tart and tangy like sour mango or apricot with a resinous, faintly pine-like note and a rich, slightly oily texture; it is always sweetened, usually with honey.

brewing.notes: Crush 50 g of fresh or thawed berries in a glass or small pot, add honey to taste and 300 ml of water at about 80 °C (boiling water dulls the fruit), stir and leave 5 minutes; drink it with the pulp. Grated ginger, a slice of orange or a cinnamon stick are the usual café additions. Dried berries: 5 g per cup, 10 minutes, boiling water.

vintage_note: Not a dried-leaf product with a vintage: it is sold as frozen berries, as berry purée or jam-like 'cheong' in jars with a production date, as a syrup for cafés, and in a smaller way as dried berries and dried leaf with a one- to two-year best-before. Fresh berries appear in markets in September and October; the café drink is made year-round from frozen stock. Look for whole bright-orange berries without a stale, rancid note, since the berry oil goes off with age.
description:
Sea buckthorn tea is the bright orange glass that every café in Kyiv, Lviv and Moscow puts on the winter menu: crushed sour-sweet berries, honey, hot water, often ginger or orange, drunk with a spoon for the pulp. The shrub grows wild on riverbanks and dunes from Europe to Mongolia, and its cultivation as a fruit crop was worked out in Siberia's Altai region, which is why Russia and Ukraine have such a habit of it.

There is no tea leaf and no processing to speak of: the berries are frozen or blended, because they are too sour and too fragile to do much else with. The berries are unusual in containing oil, which gives the drink its slightly rich, silky texture and the faint resinous, pine-like aroma that sets it apart from other sour fruit teas.

It tastes of sour mango and apricot with a tangy, almost savoury depth, and it needs honey; the balance between the two is the whole recipe. Use hot but not boiling water, crush the berries well and let it sit for a few minutes. The common mistake at home is too few berries and too much water, which gives a thin, acidic cup.

Buy frozen whole berries from a Ukrainian, Russian or Baltic grocery, or a jar of purée with a recent production date; a dried-berry infusion is milder and a dried-leaf infusion is a different, grassy drink altogether. There is no vintage, only the autumn harvest and the freezer.

It has traditionally been drunk as a winter vitamin drink; whatever you make of that, it is one of the great cold-weather cups, and it pairs naturally with ginger, orange and a little cinnamon.
sources_note: The Altai (Barnaul) origin of commercial cultivation is from general knowledge; worth a fact-check.
